title: Metabolism II
tagline: Fats, amino acids, nucleotides and light: the rest of the metabolic map, and how the body keeps it all in balance.
overview: Metabolism II continues from Metabolism I (bioenergetics, glucose metabolism, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) into the remaining major areas of metabolism: the breakdown and synthesis of lipids including cholesterol and lipoproteins, the handling of amino acid nitrogen and carbon skeletons, nucleotide synthesis and degradation, photosynthesis in plants and, finally, the integration and regulation of metabolism across organs in feeding, fasting and exercise. The split between Metabolism I and II follows the usual BSc Honours division. Throughout the course the emphasis is on pathway logic, regulation and the clinical consequences of enzyme defects.
whyItMatters: Cardiovascular disease, fatty liver, diabetes, gout, inborn errors of metabolism and cancer treatments such as methotrexate all depend on the pathways in this course. Photosynthesis connects the biochemistry of energy to agriculture and food security, and integration is the key to understanding how a whole organism, rather than a single cell, responds to a meal or a fast.
careerLinks: Clinical biochemistry and newborn metabolic screening
Pharmaceutical research on lipid-lowering, antimetabolite and anti-diabetic drugs
Nutrition science, dietetics and public health
Postgraduate research in metabolic disease, cancer metabolism and synthetic biology
studyTips: Build a one-page 'metabolic map' early in the course and add each new pathway to it in a different colour; links between pathways (acetyl-CoA, glutamate, oxaloacetate) are where most exam questions hide.
For each pathway, learn one disease or drug that interrupts it; clinical stories fix enzymes and regulation in memory much better than lists.
Practise tracing a specific carbon or nitrogen atom through several pathways; it exposes gaps in understanding quickly.
When you study regulation, always ask how the control suits the physiology of the tissue involved (liver, muscle, adipose, brain).

units.title: Fat mobilisation, beta-oxidation and ketone bodies
units.hook: Fat is the body's long-term fuel tank: more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, stored dry in adipose tissue. A marathon runner at the thirty-kilometre mark, or a person who has not eaten for three days, survives on the slow and steady burn of fatty acids that this unit follows from fat cell to mitochondrial matrix.
learningObjectives: Describe mobilisation of triacylglycerol from adipose tissue and its hormonal control
Explain activation of fatty acids and the carnitine shuttle as the regulated entry into mitochondria
Write the four reactions of the beta-oxidation spiral and calculate the ATP yield from palmitate
Explain how odd-chain and unsaturated fatty acids need extra enzymes
Describe peroxisomal oxidation and the clinical significance of defects such as MCAD deficiency
Explain ketogenesis and ketolysis, why they occur in fasting and why uncontrolled ketosis causes acidosis

keyConcepts.definition: Intracellular lipases release fatty acids and glycerol from stored triacylglycerol; glucagon and adrenaline stimulate lipolysis through cAMP and PKA while insulin suppresses it.
Activates a fatty acid to acyl-CoA at the cost of ATP converted to AMP and pyrophosphate, equivalent to two high-energy phosphate bonds.

CPT1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane converts acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine, a translocase moves it across, and CPT2 regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix; CPT1 is the regulated step and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
Four repeated reactions (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase with FAD, enoyl-CoA hydratase, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase with NAD+, thiolase) shorten the chain by two carbons as acetyl-CoA each cycle.
Palmitoyl-CoA gives seven FADH2, seven NADH and eight acetyl-CoA; with current P/O ratios the net yield is about 106 ATP after subtracting the two equivalents used for activation.

Propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids is converted via methylmalonyl-CoA (requiring biotin and vitamin B12) to succinyl-CoA, while unsaturated fatty acids need isomerase and reductase enzymes to handle cis double bonds.
Very-long-chain fatty acids and branched chains such as phytanic acid are shortened in peroxisomes, where the first oxidation produces hydrogen peroxide rather than FADH2 for the respiratory chain.
A common inborn error of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase causing fasting hypoglycaemia with low ketones, as fatty acid oxidation cannot support gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.
In liver mitochondria excess acetyl-CoA is condensed to HMG-CoA and cleaved to acetoacetate, which can be reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate or spontaneously decarboxylate to acetone.

Extrahepatic tissues such as brain, heart and muscle convert acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase, an enzyme the liver lacks, so the liver makes but cannot use ketone bodies.

deeper.beginner: When the body needs fuel between meals, fat cells release fatty acids into the blood. Muscle and liver cells take them in and chop them, two carbons at a time, into acetyl-CoA, collecting NADH and FADH2 on the way. In prolonged fasting the liver turns some acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies that the brain can use, saving glucose and muscle protein.
deeper.intermediate: Fatty acids must be activated in the cytosol but oxidised in the matrix, so the carnitine shuttle is needed, and malonyl-CoA (the first intermediate in fatty acid synthesis) inhibits CPT1 so that synthesis and oxidation do not run simultaneously in the same cell. The thiolase step uses CoA to cleave the chain, conserving the energy of the thioester. A large part of the energy yield comes from the many acetyl-CoA that go through the citric acid cycle, so fatty acid oxidation depends on adequate oxaloacetate and an intact respiratory chain. During fasting the liver makes ketones because acetyl-CoA accumulates when oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis; the brain uses ketones increasingly after several days, reducing its glucose requirement and so the breakdown of muscle protein. In diabetic ketoacidosis, lack of insulin leads to unrestrained lipolysis, ketone overproduction and a fall in blood pH.
deeper.advanced: Mitochondrial beta-oxidation uses chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenases (very-long, long, medium, short) and a trifunctional protein for long-chain substrates, which explains why defects show distinct phenotypes including cardiomyopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Electron transfer from acyl-CoA dehydrogenases goes through ETF and ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase, so defects there (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) affect many pathways. Regulation is transcriptional as well: PPAR alpha is activated by fatty acids and induces genes for oxidation and ketogenesis in fasting liver, with HMG-CoA synthase 2 as a rate-controlling step. Ketone bodies are now recognised as signalling metabolites, with beta-hydroxybutyrate inhibiting histone deacetylases and binding to receptors, as outlined in the Puchalska and Crawford review. Lipid oxidation also contributes to disease when intermediates accumulate, for example acylcarnitines in insulin resistance, so flux and capacity must be matched.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that activation costs two ATP-equivalents (ATP to AMP) and omitting it from the energy balance
Claiming that fatty acids can be converted to glucose in animals; acetyl-CoA cannot give net oxaloacetate
Saying the liver uses ketone bodies for energy; it lacks the transferase and exports them for other tissues
Confusing malonyl-CoA's role: it inhibits CPT1 and so blocks fatty acid entry to mitochondria, preventing a futile cycle with synthesis

selfCheck.question: Which molecule inhibits CPT1 and thereby prevents newly made fatty acids from being oxidised straight away?
selfCheck.explanation: Malonyl-CoA, produced by acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis, inhibits CPT1, blocking entry of acyl groups into mitochondria and avoiding a futile cycle.

selfCheck.question: How many FADH2 and NADH are produced when palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) is completely converted to acetyl-CoA?
selfCheck.explanation: Sixteen carbons need seven cleavage cycles to yield eight acetyl-CoA; each cycle gives one FADH2 and one NADH.

selfCheck.question: Why can the liver not use the ketone bodies it produces?
options: Ketone bodies cannot enter liver cells
Liver mitochondria lack the citric acid cycle
selfCheck.explanation: The liver does not express the transferase needed to activate acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA, so it exports ketone bodies for use by brain, heart and muscle.

units.title: Lipid biosynthesis, cholesterol and lipoproteins
units.hook: After a rich meal your liver turns surplus carbohydrate into fat, packages it with cholesterol into particles of VLDL and ships it to every tissue in the body. The same chain of events, when it is out of balance, narrows arteries; getting to the bottom of that story won two Nobel Prizes and gave us statins.
learningObjectives: Describe how acetyl-CoA is exported from mitochondria as citrate and how NADPH is provided for lipogenesis
Outline the reactions of acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase and how they are regulated
Explain elongation and desaturation and why linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential
Describe the synthesis of triacylglycerols and the main glycerophospholipids
Outline cholesterol biosynthesis from acetyl-CoA through mevalonate and squalene and the regulation of HMG-CoA reductase
Describe the formation and fate of chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL and the LDL receptor pathway

keyConcepts.definition: Citrate exported from mitochondria is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase to give cytosolic acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, linking carbohydrate abundance to fatty acid synthesis.

A biotin-dependent enzyme making malonyl-CoA, the committed step; it is activated by citrate and insulin-driven dephosphorylation and inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA and by AMPK or glucagon-linked phosphorylation.
In animals a large multifunctional enzyme that builds palmitate from one acetyl-CoA and seven malonyl-CoA using 14 NADPH, with the growing chain tethered to an acyl carrier protein domain.
The pentose phosphate pathway and cytosolic malic enzyme provide the reducing power for lipogenesis.
Endoplasmic reticulum enzymes extend palmitate and introduce double bonds, but humans lack enzymes for double bonds beyond carbon 9, making linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid dietary essentials.

Fatty acyl-CoA is added to glycerol 3-phosphate to form phosphatidic acid, which is dephosphorylated to diacylglycerol and then either acylated to give triacylglycerol or combined with activated head groups, such as CDP-choline, for phospholipids.
Three acetyl-CoA form HMG-CoA, which HMG-CoA reductase converts to mevalonate, followed by isoprene units, squalene and cyclisation to lanosterol and finally cholesterol.
Controlled by SREBP-2-mediated transcription, sterol-induced degradation of the enzyme, phosphorylation by AMPK and inhibition by statins, which are competitive inhibitors.

Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from gut, VLDL carries hepatic triacylglycerol, LDL (from VLDL remnants) delivers cholesterol to cells and HDL returns cholesterol to the liver in reverse transport; apolipoproteins direct receptor binding and enzyme activation.

LDL binds its receptor through apoB-100, is internalised by endocytosis and releases cholesterol, which suppresses further synthesis; defects cause familial hypercholesterolaemia, and PCSK9 promotes receptor degradation.

deeper.beginner: When we eat more energy than we use, the liver and fat cells turn the extra into fat. The raw material is acetyl-CoA, which is built up two carbons at a time into fatty acids and then attached to glycerol to make triacylglycerol. Cholesterol is also made from acetyl-CoA and is vital for membranes and hormones, but too much of it in LDL particles can lead to blocked arteries.
deeper.intermediate: Fatty acid synthesis is not the reverse of oxidation: it occurs in the cytosol, uses NADPH, malonyl-CoA and an acyl carrier protein, and is under reciprocal control with oxidation through malonyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is controlled by allosteric effectors, phosphorylation (AMPK, PKA) and long-term induction by insulin and SREBP-1c. Triacylglycerols are exported from the liver in VLDL and cleared by lipoprotein lipase, activated by apoC-II, in capillaries; the remnants give rise to LDL. HDL particles collect cholesterol from tissues and, with LCAT esterifying it, return it to the liver. The LDL receptor pathway, discovered by Brown and Goldstein, shows how receptor-mediated endocytosis regulates cell cholesterol; statins reduce hepatic synthesis, which upregulates LDL receptors and lowers plasma LDL.
deeper.advanced: HMG-CoA reductase is among the most tightly regulated enzymes known, controlled at transcription, translation, degradation (through Insig and ubiquitination in response to sterols and nonsterol isoprenoids) and phosphorylation. The two-step reduction uses two NADPH and proceeds through a thiohemiacetal, and statins mimic the HMG moiety. SREBP-1c, SREBP-2 and ChREBP are central transcriptional regulators: ChREBP responds to glucose metabolites, SREBP-1c to insulin and LXR, and SREBP-2 to cholesterol. In fatty liver disease, de novo lipogenesis is elevated and contributes to hepatic triacylglycerol accumulation despite insulin resistance in other pathways, a paradox known as selective insulin resistance. Lipoprotein metabolism is also a pharmacological hotbed: inhibitors of PCSK9 and CETP, and variants of ANGPTL3 and APOC3, show how human genetics guides drug targets, as covered in the Goldstein and Brown review.

commonMistakes: Describing fatty acid synthesis as the reverse of beta-oxidation; the enzymes, location, carrier and reductant all differ
Calling LDL 'bad' and HDL 'good' without explaining the transport direction: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues, HDL helps return it to the liver
Believing statins block the whole pathway equally; they inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, so isoprenoid products as well as cholesterol are reduced
Forgetting that ATP-citrate lyase and the citrate shuttle link lipid synthesis to the energy state of the cell

selfCheck.question: Which compound carries acetyl units from the mitochondrion to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis?
selfCheck.explanation: Acetyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane; it leaves as citrate, which ATP-citrate lyase cleaves in the cytosol back to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate.

selfCheck.question: How many NADPH are consumed to make one palmitate from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA?
selfCheck.explanation: Each of the seven rounds of elongation uses two reductive steps, each requiring one NADPH, giving fourteen in total.

Block intestinal absorption of cholesterol directly

units.title: Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle
units.hook: Ammonia is a tiny molecule that is toxic to the brain, yet your body must constantly break down amino acids and deal with the nitrogen that comes off them. The urea cycle, discovered by Hans Krebs several years before the citric acid cycle, is the liver's elegant answer to the question of how to dispose of nitrogen safely.
learningObjectives: Describe digestion of proteins and the intracellular turnover of proteins as sources of amino acids
Explain transamination and oxidative deamination, including the roles of PLP and glutamate dehydrogenase
Describe how ammonia is transported safely as glutamine and alanine
Write the reactions of the urea cycle and show where it links to the citric acid cycle
Explain the regulation of the urea cycle and the consequences of its defects
Classify amino acids as glucogenic or ketogenic and trace carbon skeletons to the seven entry points of central metabolism

keyConcepts.definition: Aminotransferases using pyridoxal phosphate shift an amino group from an amino acid to alpha-ketoglutarate, giving glutamate and a new keto acid; the reaction is freely reversible.

A mitochondrial enzyme that oxidatively deaminates glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonium, using NAD+ or NADP+; it collects nitrogen from many amino acids, and is allosterically activated by ADP and inhibited by GTP.
Free ammonia is toxic, particularly to the nervous system, so it is carried in blood in non-toxic forms such as glutamine and, from muscle, alanine.
Glutamine synthetase traps ammonia in tissues as glutamine, while the glucose-alanine cycle moves nitrogen from muscle to liver together with pyruvate carbon.
The mitochondrial regulated enzyme of the urea cycle, which makes carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP and is activated by N-acetylglutamate.

Ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase convert ornithine to citrulline, argininosuccinate, arginine and urea, regenerating ornithine; one nitrogen comes from ammonia and one from aspartate.

keyConcepts.term: Energy cost and link to citric acid cycle
keyConcepts.definition: Urea synthesis consumes four high-energy phosphate bonds per urea, and the fumarate released can enter the citric acid cycle, a connection sometimes called the Krebs bicycle.

Amino acids whose skeletons become pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates can supply glucose, while leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic and some, such as phenylalanine and tyrosine, are both.

keyConcepts.term: Inborn errors of amino acid catabolism
keyConcepts.definition: Phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase) and maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase) illustrate how a single enzyme defect disrupts a whole pathway and are detected by newborn screening.
Deficiencies of urea cycle enzymes cause hyperammonaemia with lethargy, vomiting and neurological damage, and are managed by diet and nitrogen-scavenging drugs.

deeper.beginner: When we eat more protein than we need, or break down our own proteins during fasting, the amino groups must be removed. Specific enzymes pass the amino group onto a carrier, finally forming ammonia, which the liver converts to urea, a harmless molecule that the kidneys excrete. The carbon left over is burned for energy or turned into glucose or fat.
deeper.intermediate: Most amino acids are transaminated with alpha-ketoglutarate to give glutamate, concentrating nitrogen into one molecule, whose amino group is released as ammonium by glutamate dehydrogenase in liver mitochondria. Aspartate, formed by transamination of oxaloacetate, supplies the second urea nitrogen through argininosuccinate synthetase. The first two reactions occur in mitochondria and the rest in the cytosol, which means that citrulline and ornithine must be transported across the inner membrane. The cycle is regulated at CPS I by N-acetylglutamate, whose synthesis is stimulated by arginine and by high glutamate, and by enzyme induction when protein intake is high. Branched-chain amino acids are catabolised mainly in muscle, not liver, and their keto acid dehydrogenase resembles PDH, which is why thiamine and lipoate are relevant.
deeper.advanced: PLP is a versatile cofactor forming a Schiff base (aldimine) with the lysine of the enzyme, then with the substrate, and acting as an electron sink to stabilise a carbanion intermediate; the same cofactor therefore supports transamination, decarboxylation, racemisation and elimination reactions, as detailed in the Eliot and Kirsch review. Hyperammonaemia affects the brain through glutamine accumulation in astrocytes, osmotic swelling and disruption of neurotransmitter balance. The urea cycle is only one example of nitrogen handling: in birds and reptiles uric acid is the main excretory product, and in fish ammonia is excreted directly, showing how nitrogen excretion tracks water availability. Hepatic zonation matters: periportal hepatocytes carry out the urea cycle and perivenous cells express glutamine synthetase, forming an ammonia detoxification relay. Catabolic pathways of individual amino acids are best organised by where their skeletons enter: acetyl-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA, pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate and oxaloacetate.

commonMistakes: Describing transamination as removing ammonia; it only moves the amino group, and the nitrogen is released as ammonium by deamination
Placing the entire urea cycle in the mitochondrion; the first two steps are mitochondrial and the rest are cytosolic
Forgetting that aspartate provides the second nitrogen of urea
Treating leucine as a source of glucose; as a purely ketogenic amino acid it cannot give net glucose carbon

selfCheck.question: What is the main role of glutamine in nitrogen metabolism?
options: It stores energy as a phosphate donor
It carries ammonia non-toxically in blood between tissues

units.title: Amino acid biosynthesis, one-carbon metabolism and specialised products
units.hook: Humans can make eleven of the twenty protein amino acids, and must get the other nine from food; plants and microbes can make all of them. Between those two facts sits a lot of elegant chemistry: how nitrogen gets into carbon skeletons, how single carbon atoms are passed around on folate, and how amino acids become neurotransmitters, haem and glutathione.
learningObjectives: Describe how inorganic nitrogen enters organic molecules through glutamate dehydrogenase, glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase
Explain biological nitrogen fixation and why it is energetically expensive
Outline the biosynthesis of non-essential amino acids from metabolic intermediates and list the essential amino acids
Describe the roles of tetrahydrofolate, S-adenosylmethionine and vitamin B12 in one-carbon transfers
Describe the conversion of amino acids into specialised biomolecules including haem, creatine, glutathione, catecholamines and nitric oxide
Relate defects or deficiencies, such as phenylketonuria and folate deficiency, to the underlying biochemistry

keyConcepts.definition: Certain bacteria use nitrogenase to reduce atmospheric N2 to ammonia at the cost of large amounts of ATP and reducing power, and this ammonia is the ultimate source of biological nitrogen.
Glutamine synthetase uses ATP to add ammonia to glutamate, and glutamate synthase (GOGAT) transfers the amide nitrogen to alpha-ketoglutarate, assimilating nitrogen into the amino acid pool.
Histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine cannot be synthesised by humans in adequate amounts and must be eaten.

Non-essential amino acids derive from a few intermediates: pyruvate (alanine), oxaloacetate (aspartate, asparagine), alpha-ketoglutarate (glutamate, glutamine, proline, arginine) and 3-phosphoglycerate (serine, glycine, cysteine with sulfur from methionine).
Phenylalanine hydroxylase, which uses tetrahydrobiopterin and oxygen, converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, and a defect leads to phenylketonuria.
A carrier of one-carbon units at different oxidation levels, with serine as the main donor, used in the synthesis of purines, thymidylate and methionine.
The universal methyl donor for methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins, phospholipids and small molecules, made from methionine and ATP.
Methionine synthase uses B12 to transfer a methyl group from methyl-THF to homocysteine, regenerating methionine; B12 deficiency traps folate and causes megaloblastic anaemia.

Glycine and succinyl-CoA give haem, arginine and glycine give creatine, glutamate-cysteine-glycine make glutathione, tyrosine gives catecholamines, tryptophan gives serotonin and arginine gives nitric oxide.
Homocysteine condenses with serine to eventually give cysteine, so cysteine is conditionally essential depending on methionine supply, and defects raise homocysteine.

deeper.beginner: Plants and bacteria build all their amino acids from simple starting materials, but humans have lost the ability to make about half of them, so we depend on protein in the diet. The nitrogen comes from ammonia, which is attached to carbon skeletons borrowed from sugar breakdown. Amino acids are also raw materials for many other molecules, such as haem in blood, adrenaline and the neurotransmitter serotonin.
deeper.intermediate: Assimilation of ammonia into glutamate and glutamine is the gateway, and from these two almost all other nitrogen enters amino acids by transamination. The pathways for non-essential amino acids are short and run off central intermediates, whereas pathways for essential amino acids are long and often absent in animals. Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units at the oxidation levels of methyl, methylene, methenyl and formyl, supplying carbon for purine rings, thymidylate and the regeneration of methionine. The methyl-folate trap explains why vitamin B12 deficiency produces a functional folate deficiency, and why folic acid supplements can mask the haematological sign of B12 deficiency. Specialised products illustrate how a few amino acids support large biochemical areas: haem, neurotransmitters, creatine, glutathione and nitric oxide.
deeper.advanced: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase, together with the glycine cleavage system, is a major supplier of one-carbon units, and the compartmentalised mitochondrial and cytosolic one-carbon pathways are active in proliferating cells, as described by Ducker and Rabinowitz. Antifolates such as methotrexate inhibit dihydrofolate reductase and so deplete THF for thymidylate and purine synthesis, exploiting the high demand of dividing cells. Phenylalanine hydroxylase depends on tetrahydrobiopterin, so BH4 synthesis defects can cause hyperphenylalaninaemia that does not respond to dietary restriction alone. Methylation reactions linked to SAM feed into epigenetic regulation, making one-carbon metabolism a link between diet and gene expression. Glutamine is also a major anaplerotic and nitrogen donor in rapidly dividing cells, and glutaminase is a target in cancer research.

commonMistakes: Listing the essential amino acids as fixed for all circumstances; some, like arginine, are conditionally essential in growth or illness
Treating folate and vitamin B12 as unrelated; the methionine synthase reaction ties them together
Believing humans fix nitrogen; only certain prokaryotes carry nitrogenase
Forgetting that cysteine's sulfur comes from methionine in mammals

selfCheck.explanation: Valine is one of the nine essential amino acids. Alanine and serine are made from glycolytic intermediates, and tyrosine is made from phenylalanine.

selfCheck.question: Why can vitamin B12 deficiency cause a megaloblastic anaemia that resembles folate deficiency?
options: B12 is a precursor of folate
Methionine synthase needs B12, so folate is trapped as methyl-THF and is unavailable for nucleotide synthesis
B12 is needed to absorb dietary folate in the gut
selfCheck.explanation: Without B12, methyl-THF cannot donate its methyl group to homocysteine, so the folate pool is trapped and THF forms needed for purines and thymidylate run short.

units.title: Nucleotide metabolism
units.hook: Every time a cell divides, it must make about six billion new nucleotides for its DNA alone, along with many more for RNA, ATP and signalling molecules. This demand is so characteristic of fast-growing cells that several of the most important cancer, antiviral and immunosuppressive drugs work simply by interfering with nucleotide biosynthesis.
learningObjectives: Distinguish de novo and salvage pathways for purine and pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis
Outline de novo purine synthesis from PRPP to IMP and the branches to AMP and GMP
Outline de novo pyrimidine synthesis and the formation of UMP, CTP and dTMP
Explain the roles of ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase and how they are regulated and targeted by drugs
Describe purine and pyrimidine degradation, including uric acid formation
Relate clinical conditions such as gout, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and ADA-SCID to specific enzyme defects

keyConcepts.definition: 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, made from ribose 5-phosphate and ATP, is the activated ribose donor for de novo purine synthesis, pyrimidine synthesis and salvage reactions.
The purine ring is built step by step on the ribose phosphate of PRPP using glycine, glutamine, aspartate, formate carried on THF and CO2, to produce IMP, which is converted to AMP and GMP.
The committed step of the pathway is inhibited by purine nucleotides, and the branch to AMP and GMP is cross-regulated, with GTP promoting AMP synthesis and ATP promoting GMP synthesis.
The pyrimidine ring is assembled first from carbamoyl phosphate (made by cytosolic CPS II) and aspartate to give orotate, and only then attached to ribose from PRPP to form OMP and then UMP.
Free bases are reattached to PRPP by enzymes such as HGPRT and APRT, which saves energy and is crucial in tissues with a limited capacity for de novo synthesis.

Converts ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates through a radical mechanism; its activity and specificity are controlled by ATP and dATP and by substrate-specific allosteric effectors.

Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP to dTMP using methylene-THF, converting it to dihydrofolate, which DHFR then reduces back to THF; inhibitors of these enzymes (5-fluorouracil, methotrexate) are anticancer drugs.
Purine nucleotides are degraded to hypoxanthine and xanthine and then to uric acid by xanthine oxidase, which is excreted in urine; overproduction or under-excretion causes hyperuricaemia and gout.
A severe X-linked disorder caused by HGPRT deficiency, in which failed salvage leaves excess PRPP and purines, resulting in uric acid overproduction and neurological features.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes accumulation of deoxyadenosine and dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and kills lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency.

deeper.beginner: Nucleotides are the building blocks of DNA and RNA, and also the carriers of energy such as ATP. Cells can build them from scratch using simple molecules like amino acids and CO2, or recycle the bases released from broken-down nucleic acids. Because rapidly dividing cells need so many nucleotides, drugs that block these pathways can slow cancers and infections.
deeper.intermediate: In purine synthesis the ring is constructed atom by atom on PRPP, a strategy that is different from pyrimidine synthesis, where the ring is assembled first and then joined to ribose. Both pathways use glutamine, aspartate, CO2 and ATP, and folate derivatives contribute carbon to the purine ring and to thymidylate. Feedback inhibition at PRPP synthetase and the amidotransferase prevents wasteful overproduction, while carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II in animals is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP. Deoxyribonucleotides are made by reducing ribonucleoside diphosphates, a step that is tightly regulated so that the four dNTPs are balanced; dTMP requires the additional methylation of dUMP. Purine catabolism ends in uric acid in humans, so that excess urate crystals can form in joints and cause gout, a condition treated with allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
deeper.advanced: Ribonucleotide reductase of class I uses a tyrosyl radical generated by a di-iron centre, abstracts a hydrogen atom from the ribose 3' carbon and relies on thioredoxin or glutaredoxin to regenerate its active-site cysteines, as detailed in the Nordlund and Reichard review. Its two allosteric sites, one controlling overall activity (ATP versus dATP) and one controlling specificity, let the cell coordinate dNTP pools; imbalances increase mutation rates. De novo purine enzymes can cluster into a dynamic complex called the purinosome in cells under purine demand, suggesting substrate channelling, an area reviewed by Pedley and Benkovic. Pyrimidine synthesis in mammals uses the multifunctional CAD protein (CPS II, aspartate transcarbamylase, dihydroorotase) that is regulated by phosphorylation downstream of growth signalling (mTORC1 via S6K1), linking nucleotide supply to growth. Drugs such as mycophenolic acid (IMP dehydrogenase) and leflunomide (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) exploit the dependence of lymphocytes on de novo synthesis.

commonMistakes: Saying the purine ring is made free and then attached to ribose; it is built on PRPP, unlike pyrimidines
Placing carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II in the mitochondria; the pyrimidine enzyme is cytosolic and uses glutamine, not the urea-cycle CPS I with ammonia
Assuming deoxyribonucleotides are made from deoxyribose sugars; they come from reduction of ribonucleotides
Treating uric acid as a waste product that is simply harmful; it is a normal end product and an antioxidant, harmful only in excess or when poorly excreted

selfCheck.question: Which statement about de novo purine synthesis is correct?
options: The purine ring is built stepwise on a ribose phosphate backbone provided by PRPP
The base is synthesised first and then added to ribose
Carbamoyl phosphate is the starting point
It occurs only in the mitochondria
selfCheck.explanation: Purine synthesis begins by converting PRPP to phosphoribosylamine and building up the ring on it, producing IMP as the first fully formed nucleotide.

selfCheck.question: Allopurinol is used to treat gout because it inhibits:
selfCheck.explanation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

selfCheck.question: Methotrexate impairs DNA synthesis mainly by inhibiting:
options: Dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate and purines
selfCheck.explanation: Methotrexate is a folate analogue that blocks DHFR, so cells cannot regenerate tetrahydrofolate and the supply of one-carbon units for dTMP and purine synthesis falls.

units.title: Photosynthesis: light reactions and carbon fixation
units.hook: Almost all the energy that runs the biosphere, including the rice on your plate and the tea in your cup, enters through one enzyme and one membrane: Rubisco, fixing carbon dioxide, and the thylakoid membrane, turning light into chemical energy. It is respiration run in reverse, with sunlight paying the energy bill.
learningObjectives: Describe the organisation of the thylakoid membrane and the components of photosystems I and II
Trace electron flow in the Z-scheme and explain where water is oxidised, NADPH is made and a proton gradient is generated
Explain photophosphorylation by chloroplast ATP synthase and the role of cyclic electron flow
Write the three stages of the Calvin cycle (carboxylation, reduction, regeneration) and the ATP and NADPH requirement per CO2
Explain how the Calvin cycle is regulated by light
Explain photorespiration and compare C3, C4 and CAM strategies

keyConcepts.definition: The internal membrane system of chloroplasts, housing photosystems, cytochrome b6f and ATP synthase, with light-driven proton pumping into the thylakoid lumen.
Uses light energy absorbed at P680 to oxidise water at a manganese-calcium cluster, releasing oxygen and protons and passing electrons to plastoquinone.
Transfers electrons from plastoquinol to plastocyanin and pumps protons into the lumen, analogous to Complex III in mitochondria.
Light absorbed at P700 energises electrons that pass through ferredoxin to ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase, which reduces NADP+ to NADPH.
The zig-zag energy diagram of non-cyclic electron flow showing two light-driven steps that raise electrons from water to NADPH.
The proton gradient across the thylakoid, largely a pH difference, drives chloroplast ATP synthase to make ATP in the stroma, using the same chemiosmotic principle as in mitochondria.
Electrons from photosystem I return to cytochrome b6f, making ATP without NADPH or oxygen and adjusting the ATP to NADPH ratio.
Ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase fixes CO2 onto ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate to give two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate; it is slow, abundant and also reacts with oxygen.

Carboxylation, reduction of 3-phosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate with ATP and NADPH, and regeneration of ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate; fixing three CO2 to make one triose phosphate needs nine ATP and six NADPH.
Light raises stromal pH and Mg2+, reduces thioredoxin through ferredoxin, and activates Rubisco via Rubisco activase, so the Calvin cycle is active only when ATP and NADPH are being produced.

Oxygenation of RuBP produces 2-phosphoglycolate, which must be salvaged at an energetic cost; C4 plants concentrate CO2 in bundle sheath cells using PEP carboxylase, while CAM plants separate carbon capture (night) from fixation (day).

deeper.beginner: Photosynthesis has two linked parts. In the light reactions, chlorophyll absorbs light, splits water to release oxygen, and the energy is stored in ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, enzymes use that ATP and NADPH to turn carbon dioxide from the air into sugar. Plants then use that sugar as fuel and as building material.
deeper.intermediate: The light reactions mirror respiration in reverse: electrons move from water (via photosystem II, plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f, plastocyanin, photosystem I) to NADP+, with protons accumulating in the lumen, because water splitting and plastoquinol oxidation both release protons there. The proton-motive force is mostly a pH gradient, because counter-ion movements dissipate the electrical component, and the chloroplast ATP synthase uses it, giving roughly 14 protons per three ATP in the chloroplast c-ring. The Calvin cycle needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2, which means the cycle needs a larger ATP supply than non-cyclic flow alone gives, a gap that cyclic flow helps close. Rubisco's oxygenase activity at current atmospheric concentrations wastes carbon, which C4 and CAM plants avoid by concentrating CO2; this is why sugarcane and maize (C4) and pineapple (CAM) do well in hot, dry climates.
deeper.advanced: The oxygen-evolving complex cycles through S-states and Umena and colleagues' crystal structure at 1.9 angstroms revealed a Mn4CaO5 cluster with surrounding water molecules, which gives mechanistic insight into water oxidation. Photoprotection mechanisms, such as non-photochemical quenching with the PsbS protein and the xanthophyll cycle, dissipate excess excitation energy to avoid photodamage. Rubisco is the most abundant enzyme on Earth, with a mass estimated in hundreds of millions of tonnes as estimated by Bar-On and Milo, yet it has a low turnover, a feature that has driven interest in engineering photosynthesis for higher crop yield, as reviewed by Ort and colleagues. Calvin cycle control involves thioredoxin-mediated reduction of several enzymes (fructose bisphosphatase, sedoheptulose bisphosphatase, phosphoribulokinase) and the CP12 regulatory protein, which links enzyme activity to light, and the cycle's regeneration phase uses the same transketolase and transaldolase chemistry as the pentose phosphate pathway. C4 photosynthesis evolved independently many times, demonstrating convergent solutions to the Rubisco problem.

commonMistakes: Calling the Calvin cycle the 'dark reaction'; it does not use light directly but is switched on by light-driven signals and runs only in the light in most plants
Saying that the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from CO2; it comes from water
Forgetting that photosynthesis also uses a proton gradient; the chloroplast ATP synthase works like the mitochondrial one
Thinking C4 and CAM plants do not use the Calvin cycle; they concentrate CO2 and then use the same Rubisco-based cycle

selfCheck.question: Where does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come from?
selfCheck.explanation: Photosystem II oxidises water at the manganese-calcium cluster, releasing O2, protons and electrons; the oxygen atoms of CO2 end up in carbohydrate and water.

selfCheck.question: How many ATP and NADPH are needed in the Calvin cycle to fix one CO2 into carbohydrate?
selfCheck.explanation: Fixing three CO2 to make one triose phosphate requires nine ATP and six NADPH, which is three ATP and two NADPH per CO2.

selfCheck.question: What is the advantage of C4 photosynthesis in hot, dry conditions?
options: It avoids the need for Rubisco
It concentrates CO2 around Rubisco, reducing photorespiration
It makes more ATP in the light reactions
It replaces the Calvin cycle with the pentose phosphate pathway
selfCheck.explanation: C4 plants fix CO2 first with PEP carboxylase and release it at high concentration to Rubisco in bundle sheath cells, so oxygenation by Rubisco is much reduced.

units.title: Integration and regulation of metabolism
units.hook: No cell works alone: after breakfast the liver stores, the muscles take up glucose and fat cells fill up; by the next morning the roles are reversed and the liver is feeding the brain. This final unit pulls together every pathway of the course and shows how hormones and energy sensors conduct them like an orchestra.
learningObjectives: Describe the metabolic specialisations of liver, skeletal muscle, heart, adipose tissue, brain and red blood cells
Compare metabolism in the fed state, early fasting, prolonged fasting and starvation
Explain the actions of insulin, glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol on key enzymes
Explain how AMPK and mTORC1 sense energy and nutrients and coordinate catabolism and anabolism
Describe metabolic adaptation in exercise
Explain how type 1 and type 2 diabetes represent breakdowns of metabolic integration

keyConcepts.definition: Receives all absorbed nutrients through the portal vein, buffers blood glucose, synthesises lipoproteins, ketone bodies and urea, and alters its pathways quickly in response to hormones.
Uses glucose, fatty acids and, in fasting, ketones; stores glycogen for its own use, and supplies amino acids and lactate to the liver for gluconeogenesis.
Stores triacylglycerol after meals and releases fatty acids and glycerol during fasting under hormonal control.
Depends almost entirely on glucose in the fed state and can use ketone bodies for a large share of its energy after several days of fasting; it cannot oxidise fatty acids to a significant degree.
Lack mitochondria and rely exclusively on glycolysis, so they need constant glucose supply and produce lactate for the Cori cycle.

After a meal insulin favours storage; in the first hours of fasting glycogen supplies glucose; after about a day gluconeogenesis and lipolysis dominate; in prolonged starvation ketone use spares glucose and protein.

Insulin promotes uptake and storage of fuel and inhibits lipolysis, gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; glucagon, acting mainly on liver, does the reverse; both work through second messengers and covalent modification.
Adrenaline mobilises glycogen and fat during stress or exercise, while cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis and protein breakdown over longer periods.

A kinase activated by a rising AMP/ATP ratio, which switches on ATP-producing pathways (glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation) and switches off ATP-consuming ones (fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, protein synthesis).
A kinase complex that integrates amino acid, growth factor and energy signals to promote protein, lipid and nucleotide synthesis and cell growth when nutrients are plentiful.
The ability to switch between fuels according to availability, which is impaired in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

deeper.beginner: Your organs divide the metabolic work. After you eat, insulin tells the liver, muscle and fat to store the fuel; between meals, glucagon and other hormones tell them to release it. The brain needs a steady supply of glucose, and in a long fast the liver makes ketone bodies from fat so that the brain can use those as well. When this coordination fails, as in diabetes, blood glucose and fat metabolism become dangerously unbalanced.
deeper.intermediate: Regulation operates at several time scales: allosteric effects act in seconds, covalent modification through hormone-triggered kinases and phosphatases in minutes, and changes in enzyme levels through transcription in hours to days. Insulin stimulates glucose transport in muscle and fat through GLUT4 translocation, and activates glycogen synthase, ACC and lipoprotein lipase, while suppressing hormone-sensitive lipase and gluconeogenic enzymes. During fasting, glucagon raises cAMP in liver, activating glycogen phosphorylase, then gluconeogenesis, and adipose lipolysis supplies fatty acids that fuel the liver and muscle and spare glucose for the brain. In prolonged fasting, ketone bodies reduce the brain's glucose requirement and so protein catabolism is minimised. In exercise, AMP, calcium and adrenaline combine to switch on fuel mobilisation matched to demand. In type 1 diabetes, absence of insulin leads to hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis, whereas in type 2 diabetes tissues respond poorly to insulin and the pancreas eventually fails to compensate.
deeper.advanced: AMPK is a heterotrimer sensing adenine nucleotides through its gamma subunit and activated by LKB1-mediated phosphorylation of the alpha subunit; its phosphorylation targets (ACC, HMG-CoA reductase, TSC2, raptor and ULK1) explain its coordinate switch from anabolism to catabolism, as reviewed by Hardie and colleagues. mTORC1 is recruited to lysosomes by Rag GTPases in response to amino acids and activated by Rheb in response to growth factors via the PI3K-Akt pathway, and the two kinases form a reciprocal pair, described in the Saxton and Sabatini review. Selective insulin resistance in liver, with continued lipogenesis but impaired suppression of gluconeogenesis, illustrates how branches of a signalling pathway can behave differently. Interorgan cycles such as the Cori, glucose-alanine and fatty acid-glycerol cycles allow tissues to share the metabolic burden, and metabolomics and isotope tracing now quantify these fluxes in intact organisms. A systems view treats metabolism as a regulated network where controlled variables (blood glucose, ATP, pH) are maintained by feedback, and where robustness is bought at the cost of vulnerability when several regulators fail at once.

commonMistakes: Describing hormones as acting on pathways in general; each acts on particular enzymes in particular tissues, with different effects in liver, muscle and fat
Saying the brain can use fatty acids as fuel; it uses glucose and, in prolonged fasting, ketone bodies
Treating insulin resistance and insulin deficiency as the same thing; type 1 lacks insulin and type 2 involves reduced response
Forgetting that metabolic control works on several time scales, not only by allosteric effects

selfCheck.question: During prolonged fasting, why does the brain's use of ketone bodies matter for the rest of the body?
options: It reduces the need for gluconeogenesis and so spares muscle protein
It allows the brain to oxidise fatty acids directly
selfCheck.explanation: As ketone bodies replace part of the brain's glucose requirement, less glucose has to be made from amino acids, so muscle protein breakdown is reduced.

selfCheck.question: Which of the following is an effect of AMPK activation?
options: Increased fatty acid synthesis through ACC activation
Increased fatty acid oxidation through ACC inhibition and lower malonyl-CoA
selfCheck.explanation: AMPK phosphorylates and inhibits ACC, lowering malonyl-CoA, which relieves CPT1 inhibition and favours fatty acid oxidation over synthesis.

selfCheck.question: After an overnight fast, which statement describes liver metabolism?
options: Glycogen synthesis and lipogenesis are high
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis supply glucose, and ketogenesis begins to rise
Glycolysis is the main source of ATP
selfCheck.explanation: With low insulin and high glucagon, the liver releases glucose through glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis and begins to make ketone bodies from fatty acids.
